tweets.text: Why can anyone drain some contracts? A withdrawal function without a caller check lets any account trigger a transfer of Ether out. Limit withdrawals to authorized parties. Which of your functions move Ether, and who can call them?

tweets.text: One recipient whose code always reverts can freeze a function that pays out to many addresses in a loop, because the whole batch needs every payment to succeed.
External calls can fail by accident or on purpose. When a contract needs every call in a batch to go through, a single failing recipient can block the entire operation.
Sending Ether can fail for separate reasons. The recipient may run out of gas, or its code may revert through require, assert or revert.
The two send styles fail differently. transfer reverts the sending call when the send fails, while send only returns false, so you must check its return value yourself.
Either way, a recipient that always fails can stall progress in the sending contract. The underlying problem is that progress depends on every external transfer or call succeeding.
Prefer pull payments, where users withdraw their funds instead of having them pushed automatically. This also lowers the chance of running into gas limit problems.

Isolate each external call in its own transaction that the recipient can initiate. Avoid combining several calls in one transaction, especially inside a loop, and write logic that handles failed calls.
Search your contracts for every loop that sends Ether or makes an external call, and test it with a recipient that always reverts to see whether the whole batch stalls.

tweets.text: A withdrawal function that sends Ether before it clears the caller's balance can be called back into while the balance is still unchanged, so the same funds can be withdrawn again.
Calling another contract hands it control. That contract can call back into yours before your first call has returned, and your function is then running again with half-finished state.
In the withdrawal case, the callback reads a balance that has not been reduced yet. The check passes a second time, and another payout goes out against the same stored amount.
Ether transfers are not the only way in. Reentrancy can arise from calls to any other contract, and dependencies spanning several contracts matter too.
The underlying flaw is a state update placed after an untrusted call, which lets the same logic execute repeatedly. The fix is to reorder the steps.
Checks-effects-interactions gives the order: validate inputs and permissions, update the relevant storage, and only then make external calls.

For a withdrawal, save the amount to pay, then clear the stored balance with `balances[msg.sender] = 0;` before calling the recipient. Require that call to succeed so a failure reverts the whole operation.
A callback may also enter through a different function or a dependency that shares the same state. Review every other callable path touching that state, not just the one you fixed.
Does every function that makes an external call finish updating its storage, and every path sharing that storage, before the call goes out?

tweets.text: A function that trusts the order in which transactions arrive can be made to run in a different order by anyone who pays a higher gas price. That race condition is called transaction order dependence.

The cause is that block producers pick which transactions go into a block based on gas price, and anyone running a node can see transactions before they are finalized. So shared state changes depend on an ordering others can influence.

Picture a contract that gives 1 token to the first person who solves a math problem. Alice submits the answer at a standard gas price, Eve sees it and sends the same answer with a much higher gas price, and Eve's transaction is processed first.
The ERC20 approve function has a similar problem. Alice changes Eve's allowance from n to m, and Eve sends a transferFrom of n with a higher gas price, so it lands before Alice's change.
Once Alice's transaction sets the allowance to m, Eve can spend m as well. She ends up with n + m, when the most she should get is max(n,m).
For reward-for-information cases, SWC suggests a commit-reveal scheme. The sender first submits hash(salt, address, answer), and the contract stores that hash along with the sender's address.
Later the sender submits the salt and answer. The contract recomputes hash(salt, msg.sender, answer) and releases the reward on a match, so watching the mempool does not let Eve copy the answer.

For approve, the best fix is to pass in the expected current allowance and revert on a mismatch, though that breaks ERC20 conformance. A safe approve function is an alternative, and users can set approvals to zero before changing them.
Before shipping, check whether any reward or payout goes to whoever's transaction lands first, and whether any allowance change can be front-run by a spender who sees it pending.

tweets.text: An attacker who registers a contract that always reverts as a payee can freeze a function that pays many addresses in one loop, and nobody else in that batch gets paid.
Ether sends can break for two separate reasons: the recipient runs out of gas, or the recipient's own code reverts through require, assert or revert.
Solidity's two send styles react differently to that failure. transfer reverts the calling transaction, while send just returns false, so skipping a check on its return value hides the problem.

A loop that pays everyone ties the contract's forward movement to each recipient behaving. Any payee that can fail on demand gets a lever over the sender's progress, and that is where the denial of service comes from.
Pull payments remove that lever. Users withdraw their own funds, so a broken recipient only affects itself, and this also lowers the chance of hitting gas limit trouble.

Give each external call its own transaction that the recipient starts. Keep several calls out of a single transaction, most of all inside loops, and treat every external call as something that may fail.
Grep your contracts for every loop that sends Ether or makes an external call, then run it in a test against a recipient whose code always reverts and confirm the other payments still work.

tweets.text: A function that relies on transactions arriving in a certain order can be forced to run in another order by anyone willing to pay a higher gas price. This race condition is known as transaction order dependence.

Miners pick transactions for a block based on gas price, and anyone running a node can watch transactions before they are finalized. Shared state changes therefore rest on an ordering that other parties can influence.

Imagine a contract that pays 1 token to whoever first solves a math problem. Alice sends her answer with a standard gas price. Eve spots it, resubmits the same answer with a far higher gas price, and her transaction is processed first.
ERC20 approve has a related race. Alice moves Eve's allowance from n to m. Eve sees that, submits a transferFrom for n with a higher gas price, and it gets processed before Alice's change.
After Alice's change sets the allowance to m, Eve can spend m too. Her total is n + m, where the intended ceiling was max(n,m).
For reward-for-information cases, SWC suggests a commit-reveal hash scheme. The sender first submits hash(salt, address, answer), and the contract keeps that hash together with the sender's address.
In the reveal step the sender sends the salt and the answer. The contract recomputes hash(salt, msg.sender, answer) and releases the reward only if it matches the stored hash.

For approve, SWC calls the best fix passing the expected current allowance and reverting on a mismatch, but that makes the token non-conformant with ERC20. A safe approve function is an alternative, and users can zero an approval before changing it.
Before shipping, check two things: does any reward go to whoever lands first, and can a pending allowance change be raced by a spender who sees it?

tweets.text: A withdrawal function that pays out Ether before zeroing the caller's balance can be re-entered by the recipient, and the second entry still sees the old balance.
Any external call gives the callee control of execution. It can invoke your contract again before the original call has returned, so your code runs a second time mid-operation.
Sending Ether is only one trigger. Calling any other contract can open the same door, and state shared across several contracts widens the surface further.
The flaw underneath is ordering: storage is changed only after control has been handed to code you do not trust, so the same logic can run again and again.
Checks-effects-interactions fixes the ordering. Verify inputs and permissions first, then write the new storage values, and make external calls last.

Applied to a withdrawal, copy the amount into a local variable and run `balances[msg.sender] = 0;` before paying the recipient. Also require the payment to succeed, so a failed send reverts everything.
A callback does not have to come back through the function you patched. It may enter via a different function or a dependency that touches the same state, so audit each of those paths too.
Does every function that makes an external call finish its storage updates before the call goes out?
